title: Anthropic Team Now Worth More Than Bottom Third of All US Households
content:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei gestures at the NASDAQ MarketSite in New York City on November 19, 2026, the day of the artificial intelligence company's initial public offering.
(Photo by Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)
Anthropic Team Now Worth More Than Bottom Third of All US Households, Says Investment Firm CEO
"It's OK," one observer said sardonically, "trickle-down economics will save the day."
A prominent private investment firm CEO and former White House adviser said the founders and employees of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic are collectively worth more than the bottom third of US households following Thursday's initial public offering, an eye-popping example of the country's widening wealth inequality amid the AI boom.
In a social media post, Willett Advisors chair and CEO Steven Rattner highlighted figures claiming that approximately 5,300 Anthropic founders and employees collectively hold an estimated $433 billion in wealth, slightly exceeding the $432 billion he said is held by more than 45 million least wealthy US households.
Rattner's figures are drawn from Anthropic's initial public offering (IPO) documents and the US Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances.
The numbers from Rattner—who served as lead adviser to the Presidential Task Force on the Auto Industry during the Obama administration—reflect the value of company equity, not necessarily cash or other wealth that employees can immediately access.
San Francisco-based Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, went public Thursday in what is being called the largest IPO in US history. Shares closed at $97.17, more than 17% above their $83 offering price, giving the company a market capitalization of approximately $1.75 trillion.
Earlier Thursday, CBS News estimated that Anthropic’s seven co-founders were each worth approximately $20 billion, while CNBC said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO will also make thousands of current and former Anthropic employees instant multimillionaires.
Progressive commentator Matt Stoller called the IPO "a giant payoff to a set of stakeholders for allowing them to steal the copyrights of millions of people" and "a huge theft of wealth."
Gaby Del Valle, a policy reporter at The Verge, said, "If you're a newly minted Anthropic multimillionaire, may I suggest building a library or perhaps becoming a patron of the arts."
"Do NOT talk to me about shrimp welfare, I don't wanna hear it," she added, referring to the humane seafood initiative largely funded by billionaire Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, Cari Tuna.
Del Valle wasn't the only one who turned to humor in the face of such a staggering statistic.
Responding to Rattner's post, Bland Labs founder Joshua Collin sardonically quipped on social media, "It's OK, trickle-down economics will save the day."
This country and this world are at a monumental crossroads.
US voters have an opportunity to beat back the forces of fascism and confront the billionaires who are rigging the economy, our media system, and our democracy, making it increasingly impossible for ordinary people to get by.
We’re not just talking about the election. We’re talking about what must be done once these fascist elements are vanquished from power. We need a bolder set of solutions than what either major party has so far been willing to offer and a working-class movement ready to fight like hell for it.
Trump didn't emerge from nowhere. The conditions that fueled MAGA authoritarianism were created by decades of radical neoliberal economic policies and a corrupt political system dominated by corporate interests.
They slashed taxes on the super-rich, promising that the benefits would trickle down. They said giveaways to the corporate titans would make life more affordable for the rest of us.
It was all bullshit. And when a bitter, betrayed populace searches for someone to blame, right-wing demagogues have little trouble finding scapegoats.
People know when they're being lied to, but you won't hear any of this from the corporate media. Only independent journalism—powered and funded by people who believe in building a better world—can deliver truly trustworthy daily news.

report.summary: Anthropic’s post-IPO equity has made roughly 5,300 founders and employees worth about $433B—more than the poorest third of US households—spotlighting AI-boom inequality.
report.background: Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind the Claude chatbot, went public in what is being called the largest US IPO in history. Shares priced at $83 and closed at $97.17, valuing the company at about $1.75 trillion. The wealth comparison comes from investor Steven Rattner, who cited IPO documents and the Federal Reserve’s 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances. The figures reflect company equity, not immediately accessible cash. The IPO has made many early employees and founders paper billionaires or multimillionaires, intensifying debate about who captures the gains from the AI boom, copyright disputes, and widening US wealth inequality.
key_points: Rattner says about 5,300 Anthropic founders and employees collectively hold roughly $433 billion, slightly more than the $432 billion held by more than 45 million least-wealthy US households. The comparison is striking because it sets a few thousand AI workers against a large slice of the US population.

Anthropic’s IPO was priced at $83 per share and closed at $97.17, up more than 17%, giving the company a market capitalization of approximately $1.75 trillion. CBS News estimated each of the seven co-founders was worth about $20 billion, while CNBC said thousands of employees became instant multimillionaires.

The figures are based on equity value, not liquid cash. Employees may face lockup periods, taxes, and share-price swings, so the headline wealth is paper wealth. Still, the comparison with Federal Reserve household-wealth data has become a viral symbol of AI-driven inequality.

Critics responded sharply. Progressive commentator Matt Stoller called the IPO a payoff for “stealing the copyrights of millions of people,” while others used sardonic humor about trickle-down economics. Supporters would likely emphasize innovation, job creation, and the risky, long-term nature of building AI companies.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Anthropic’s IPO signals that frontier AI labs can command public-market valuations rivaling the largest tech companies, encouraging more AI startups to chase scale and eventually go public. For developers, the wealth concentration may intensify competition for talent and reinforce the power of a few model providers, while open-source alternatives become more important for cost and independence. For regular users, the boom promises more capable assistants but also raises concerns about pricing, dependence on a handful of companies, copyright, and political backlash over inequality. The IPO may also invite greater regulatory scrutiny of AI firms’ data practices and market power.
report.tools: To follow the story, watch SEC EDGAR for Anthropic filings, the Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances and Inequality.org for wealth data, and OpenSecrets for lobbying. To try alternatives to Claude, explore Hugging Face, Ollama, OpenRouter, and open models such as Llama, Mistral, and Qwen.
